angle: Volume for volume's sake worked in 2022. Here's what works now.
post_first_line: 8 minutes. Zach Herman's entire outreach flow.
linkedin_post:
8 minutes. Zach Herman's entire outreach flow.

The time it freed up matters less than what it protected.

Zach Herman said the saved time can go to more volume, mid-funnel deals, or enablement with reps on the team. Through all of it, the quality of the outreach stays very high.

Zach's take on volume: volume for the sake of volume worked awesome in 2022. Back then, Zach loaded up Outreach and sent 1,000 emails a day out of a primary mailbox, and it worked great.

That doesn't work today.

What works now is quality volume, done at scale.

Personalization at scale comes up constantly. Zach Herman's point is that this kind of flow is how it actually gets accomplished.

What changed most in your outbound since 2022?

The goal now is quality volume that can still run at scale.
Time saved on outreach can go to mid-funnel deals or enablement for reps.

angle: I tried stitching ChatGPT and Claude into my outbound. It was worse than doing it by hand.
post_first_line: 10 to 12 hour days were the old outbound.
linkedin_post:
10 to 12 hour days were the old outbound.

Zach Herman tried to fix it with the tools everyone reaches for, and the result surprised even the person who built it.

In the past, Zach used ChatGPT and Claude and tried to stitch them together to make outbound as easy as possible. At the end of the day, the output was not even remotely as good as the work done manually.

The manual work was the problem too. It forced Zach into 10 to 12 hour days, just trying to write stronger emails or make more targeted calls.

Now the same work happens in a couple of minutes. The part Zach keeps hammering on: the quality stays so strong.

It also picks up on almost all of Zach's context. That was the missing piece when stitching tools together.

Speed was never the hard part. Faster output that's worse than what you'd do by hand just creates more work to fix.

takeaways: Stitching general AI tools together produced outbound that was worse than manual work for Zach Herman.
Long manual days were the cost of keeping quality high.
The real test of any outbound system is whether quality holds while time drops and context carries over.

caption: Worse than doing it manually

angle: The 17-title Boolean search SDRs still run, and what replaced it
post_first_line: 17 job titles in one Boolean search.
linkedin_post:
17 job titles in one Boolean search.

That was the old way Zach Herman built contact lists, and the part that came next is what really cost the time.

Zach Herman used to go through 25 accounts one by one in LinkedIn Sales Navigator. Each one got a crazy Boolean string with 17 different titles, and then it was a matter of hoping it pulled all of them.

If the search didn't turn up enough contacts, the whole thing got run again. Then the results got pushed back to ZoomInfo, and the same process started over.

The new workflow looks different. Zach Herman took the top 10 contacts from the list to keep it simple, and the suggestions came back without a custom search string.

The ranking is where it gets interesting. You set the criteria yourself, like funding amount or how many jobs a company is hiring for. Then you can rank on something like "hiring for more than 200 jobs and raised a Series C in the last 3 months."

The old process was a search problem. The new one is a prioritization problem.

What's the longest Boolean string you've ever written?

lesson.title: From Boolean searches to ranked contacts
takeaways: The old workflow meant one Boolean search per account, with 17 titles each, and hoping it caught everyone.
Coming up short meant repeating the search and pushing results back to ZoomInfo.
Ranking on your own criteria, like funding amount or number of open jobs, replaces guesswork with prioritization.
lesson.exercise: Pick 10 target accounts and write down the two signals that would make one a priority, such as funding stage or hiring volume. Rank the list on those signals before you search for any contacts.

angle: I tried ChatGPT as an SDR and it made my outreach slower, not faster
post_first_line: Zach Herman tried ChatGPT as an SDR.
linkedin_post:
Zach Herman tried ChatGPT as an SDR.

It made outreach slower, not faster.

This was around 2022 or '23, when the first version of ChatGPT came out. Zach Herman still had the full stack: outreach tools, Zoom info, Sales Nav, Six Sense, Demandbase.

Then AI got thrown into the mix and everybody tried to use it effectively.

The problem was that it wasn't purpose-built for sellers.

Zach Herman tried to get it to write better basic copy. It didn't remember how Zach talks. It never sounded right.

So getting the tool to write copy the right way took more time than writing it. The effort to make AI faster turned into doing the work manually again.

A tool that saves no time is just another tab to manage.

Where has AI slowed down your outreach?

Slide 6: It didn't remember how Zach talks or writes.
Slide 7: Prompting it took longer than writing the copy manually.
Slide 8: If a tool doesn't save time, it's just another tab.

lesson.title: When AI Slows You Down
takeaways: General-purpose AI isn't built for sellers, and the gap shows up fast.
If the tool doesn't capture how you sound, you'll end up rewriting its output.
The test of an AI tool is time saved, not novelty.
lesson.exercise: Time yourself writing one outreach message manually, then time getting AI to produce one you'd actually send. Keep the tool only if it wins.

caption: AI made my outreach slower

angle: The 6-tool prospecting workflow most AEs are a little embarrassed to admit they used to run
linkedin_post:
Six tools. One prospecting workflow.

Speaker D admits it's a little embarrassing to look back on, but it's probably what a lot of people were doing.

The process started in Salesforce, building a report of accounts to reach out to. Next came LinkedIn Sales Nav to find prospects at each account and build a list.

Then ZoomInfo imported that list back into Salesforce. After that, those people were added to Outreach, a sequence was created, and the emails went out.

Because the process was so long, there was not nearly as much personalization as there should have been. It turned into a spray and pray strategy.

Speaker D says things are in a much better spot now.

The workflow wasn't the only problem. The time it took pushed reps toward volume over relevance.

What did your old prospecting workflow look like?
carousel: Slide 1: Six tools just to send one prospecting email.
Slide 2: Step one: build an account report in Salesforce.
Slide 3: Step two: find prospects in LinkedIn Sales Nav.
Slide 4: Step three: import the list with ZoomInfo, back to Salesforce.
Slide 5: Step four: add people to Outreach and build a sequence.
Slide 6: The process was so long that personalization suffered.
Slide 7: The result was a spray and pray strategy.
Slide 8: Speaker D says we're now in a much better spot.

lesson.title: When the workflow is long, personalization is the first thing to go
takeaways: A multi-step process across Salesforce, Sales Nav, ZoomInfo and Outreach left little room for personalization.
Long workflows pushed reps toward spray and pray outreach.
Many reps were likely running the same process, so there's nothing to be embarrassed about.
lesson.exercise: Write down every tool and handoff between picking an account and sending the email. Count the steps, then circle the one that most limits how personalized your outreach can be.

angle: Strategic account research used to take weeks. I built a full plan and sequence in 3 minutes.
post_first_line: 3 minutes. Full outbound plan and sequence.
linkedin_post:
3 minutes. Full outbound plan and sequence.
Zach Herman used to work strategic accounts as an SDR, and the research was the part nobody talked about.

Back then, Zach Herman would read 10K reports just to send one email. Hours on end of research for a single account.

You could spend weeks figuring out who to reach out to at a company like Nike and how to tee up the outreach.

In a recent demo, Zach Herman built a full outbound plan and sequence for a massive account in about 3 minutes. Then gave it one more once over and pushed the contacts directly into the sequence.

The teams we've heard from say they're going from list to sequence 90% faster. The end-to-end outbound workflow is what makes that possible, not any single step.

The research hasn't stopped mattering. It just doesn't have to eat weeks anymore.
